description: Hola Somos ESTRELLA DEL NORTE. Encaramos el desafío NASA de resiliencia agrícola. Nuestra visión: ayudar y colaborar interconectando información disponible a múltiples áreas que puedan serle de utilidad, explotando al máximo los recursos tecnológicos. Ya tenemos 1 integrante con conocimientos técnicos. Faltan 5 tripulantes para esta misión interdisciplinaria de 48hs. Sumate a hacer la diferencia!
summary:
Every autumn, farmers in the dry Chaco of Santiago del Estero, Argentina, face the same question: plant a winter crop that protects the soil but spends stored water, or leave the field fallow, saving water but leaving the soil bare to wind and sun? AgroOrbit turns NASA Earth observations into an answer for one specific field.

The farmer draws a field on a map. In four steps the app shows which NASA data cover it, six seasons of HLS satellite greenness with the days the soil was bare, how full the soil's water tank is this autumn compared with every autumn since 2000 (GLDAS and SMAP), and at least three rotations. Each rotation is ranked by the farmer's priorities and replayed through a FAO-56 water-balance model with real NASA POWER weather, including the 2008/09 drought. Each one gets a traffic light and a 5-point card: why, evidence, benefits, missing information and risks.

Every number shows its source and date. The tool runs on global NASA data, works in Argentina today, and supports the judgment of farmers and agronomists; it never replaces it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AgroOrbit Field Shift is a decision-support web app for one decision: what to do with a field in the autumn window, and what that choice means for the next seasons. The pilot is Bandera, in the rainfed southeast of Santiago del Estero, Argentina, where water is the limiting factor and our sample field stayed bare 226 to 272 days a season in the last four seasons. Kansas and Iowa work as contrast zones, so the same flow can be compared with wetter, well-studied farmland.

The user walks through four steps:

1. Your field. Draw a polygon on a map with live NASA GIBS layers (HLS reflectance, MODIS NDVI, SMAP root-zone moisture, IMERG rainfall). The app returns the area, the zone, and which datasets actually cover the field. Outside the precomputed zones it says "no data" instead of borrowing numbers from somewhere else. Fields the user draws are saved in their own browser, with no account needed, and example fields are always there to try.

2. Field history. Fortnightly HLS NDVI at 30 m, clipped to the field, for every season since 2020: crops per year, bare-soil days, and the windows when the soil is most exposed.

3. Soil water. How full the top meter of soil is in the decision month (April in the south, October in the north), as a percentile against every year since 2000 (GLDAS), plus today's SMAP reading and the three past autumns that started most alike ("analog years").

4. Rotations. The current rotation against at least two alternatives (for example, soybean with winter fallow, soybean with a winter cover crop, or maize/sorghum with wheat or chickpea). The farmer sets priorities (save water, stop erosion, add organic matter, add nitrogen, forage, income) and constraints (irrigation, machinery, market). The ranking updates live. Each rotation gets a traffic light per priority and a 5-point card: why, evidence, benefits, missing information, and risks for an expert to check.

The tool also includes a printable one-page summary to take to the agronomist, a "How we know this" page explaining each source and where it stops being useful, a plain-language glossary (evapotranspiration, NDVI, soil-moisture anomaly, water balance), and full English/Spanish support.

HOW IT WORKS

- Precompute pipeline (Python): downloads each NASA source for the study zones and publishes analysis-ready files (Parquet and Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF) to object storage. HLS v2.0 L30 and S30 are combined into fortnightly cloud-free NDVI median composites on a shared 30 m UTM grid. NASADEM gives slope on that same grid. SMAP L4 and GLDAS are read through NASA CMR and OPeNDAP. NASA POWER provides daily weather since 1981. SoilGrids gives plant-available water per soil layer (Saxton & Rawls).

- Stateless API (FastAPI): reads only the precomputed files. It clips 30 m rasters to the field polygon. It uses POWER, GLDAS and SMAP only as zone context, and it never mixes absolute values between products; it compares percentiles within each one. Every value travels with its provenance: source, resolution, date, uncertainty range, and whether it was measured by a satellite, computed by a reanalysis, or estimated by a model.

- Water model: a daily FAO-56 soil-water bucket. Rain comes from POWER, reference evapotranspiration from Hargreaves on POWER temperatures, crop coefficients by crop and stage, and the tank size from SoilGrids. It replays each rotation through real past seasons (backtesting), not a forecast. In Bandera's sample field, the soil water left at soybean sowing in the 2008/09 drought is 75 mm after a winter fallow and 46 mm after a winter cover crop; in the wettest season on record (2002/03) it is 162 mm and 106 mm. Each replay carries a confidence level: medium for the drought, low for wet seasons. That gap, and how far to trust it, is the trade-off the farmer has to weigh.

- Front end (Nuxt, static SPA): a four-step guided flow on a map, built mobile-first, with an accessible traffic light (shape plus color plus text).

VALIDATION AND HONEST LIMITS

- GLDAS against SMAP in Bandera (25 overlapping months, 2017-2019): correlation 0.85 with almost identical means, so GLDAS extends the soil-water history back to 2000.

- Bucket model against SMAP, computed by the app over the continuous 2015-2026 daily series (GET /api/v1/validacion): r = 0.54 in Bandera (0.53 in dry seasons, 0.43 in wet ones), 0.72 in Kansas and 0.65 in Iowa. In Bandera's wet seasons the bucket fills up about 25 days per season, against 1 day in dry ones, and discards the rain it cannot hold, because it does not model deep drainage, the water table or the native forest. The worst wet season, 2018/19, reaches only r = 0.18. That is why wet-season replays come out with low confidence and the 2008/09 drought with medium confidence.

- NASA POWER overestimates rainfall in Santiago del Estero (about 807 mm against about 575 mm from local records), so the app uses anomalies and percentiles, not raw millimeters.

- SoilGrids clay in our sample field ranges from 1% to 76% (5-95% interval), so the 5-point card lists a soil test as missing information.

- In the Chaco, SRTM shows forest canopy as false hills; the app uses bare-soil days from HLS to measure wind-erosion exposure instead of relying on slope.

BENEFITS AND WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

- A farmer or advisor gets, in minutes, a field-specific view that today requires several tools, a GIS analyst and US-only datasets.

- The trade-off between water today and soil tomorrow becomes visible and quantified with real seasons, not abstract advice.

- Every recommendation explains itself and says where local judgment is needed, which builds trust with farmers who are rightly skeptical of black boxes.

- It works where US-centric tools do not. Field Shift replaces SSURGO, CDL and PRISM with global NASA data and points to the Argentine equivalents (INTA Soil Map, INTA National Crop Map, MapBiomas Argentina, INTA and SMN weather stations).

- Next steps: validate the rotation logic with INTA Quimilí/Bandera agronomists, add a wet-season drainage term to the bucket, calibrate rainfall with local stations, add more zones of the Argentine Chaco, and offer an optional Google sign-in with a Cloudflare D1 database so saved fields sync across devices.

TOOLS

Python 3.13, FastAPI, Pydantic, pandas, PyArrow, NumPy, SciPy, h5py, rasterio, odc-stac, pystac-client, shapely, pyproj, pytest; Nuxt 4, Vue 3, TypeScript, Leaflet with Leaflet-Geoman, Nuxt i18n, openapi-fetch; Docker, Caddy on a VPS, Cloudflare R2, rclone; GitLab. Data access through NASA Earthdata (CMR, OPeNDAP), NASA GIBS WMTS, the NASA POWER API, Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC (HLS, NASADEM) and the ISRIC SoilGrids WCS.

Project deployed and operational: https://agroorbit.earth/

Source code: https://gitlab.com/experimentos_sgo/field-shift

Documentation (wiki): https://gitlab.com/experimentos_sgo/field-shift/-/wikis/home
dataRefs: HLS - Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, v2.0 HLSL30
HLS - Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, v2.0 HLSS30, 30 m.
SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9 km Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP), v008.
GLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4, monthly 0.25 degree, v2.1 (GLDAS_NOAH025_M).
NASA POWER - daily meteorology (MERRA-2 based), 1981 to present.
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services) WMTS.
projectRefs: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-2 MSI: half of the HLS observations (HLSS30) come from Sentinel-2, harmonized by NASA with Landsat.

CONAE (National Space Activities Commission of Argentina), SAOCOM 1A/1B L-band soil moisture: evaluated as a second opinion on soil moisture. It covers the core Pampas but not the Bandera pilot area (nearest coverage about 35 km away), so the app shows it as "not available" there rather than inventing a value.
ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0 (250 m): sand, silt, clay, organic carbon and their 5-95% uncertainty range; plant-available water computed with Saxton & Rawls (2006).
Allen, R. G., Pereira, L. S., Raes, D., Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56.

Argentine reference equivalents for US-only datasets (cited in the app, not processed): INTA Soil Map (Carta de Suelos), INTA National Crop Map, MapBiomas Argentina, INTA and SMN weather stations, MAGyP agricultural estimates, FAO GAEZ.
